glossary.definition: Toward the front. In the brain this is toward the forehead.
Toward the back.
Above another part; toward the top of the head.
Below another part.
Toward the midline that divides left from right.
Toward the side, away from the midline.
Farther from the surface.
Closer to the surface.
A cut that splits a structure into left and right parts.
Also called frontal: a cut that splits a structure into front and back parts.
A horizontal cut that splits a structure into upper and lower parts (the app's Axial slider).
In the brain, toward the top; in the spinal cord, toward the back.
In the brain, toward the bottom; in the spinal cord, toward the front.
On the opposite side. Example: the right motor cortex controls the left side of the body.
On the same side.
A ridge on the folded surface of the brain (plural: gyri).
A groove between two gyri (plural: sulci).
The thin outer sheet of the cerebrum; the word comes from the Latin for bark.
A bundle of axons in white matter that carries signals between regions.
One half (left or right) of the cerebrum; together the hemispheres make up most of the brain.

beginner.summary: The adult brain is usually described as four big regions. Learning these four first gives you a map for everything else.

points.text: The four major regions are the cerebrum, the diencephalon, the brain stem, and the cerebellum.
The wrinkled outer layer of the cerebrum is the cerebral cortex. Its folding packs a large surface into the skull.
A deep groove, the longitudinal fissure, splits the cerebrum into left and right hemispheres.
Many control relationships are crossed: the right motor cortex moves the left side of the body.

expert.summary: Developmentally, the forebrain (prosencephalon) divides into telencephalon and diencephalon, the midbrain stays undivided, and the hindbrain (rhombencephalon) becomes the metencephalon and myelencephalon. The app's group hierarchy follows this scheme.

points.text: The cerebral hemispheres derive from the telencephalon and make up roughly 85% of brain mass.
The ventricles are remnants of the neural tube's cavity: lateral ventricles (telencephalon), third ventricle (diencephalon), fourth ventricle (rhombencephalon).

checks.q: Which list names the four major regions of the adult brain?
options: Cortex, white matter, ventricles, spinal cord
checks.explain: Frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital are lobes of the cerebrum, one of the four regions.

beginner.summary: The frontal lobe sits at the front of each hemisphere, in front of the central sulcus. It is mainly about movement, planning, and thinking.

points.text: The central sulcus separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe behind it.
Its back strip, the precentral gyrus, is the primary motor cortex.
The prefrontal cortex at the front supports functions behind personality, short-term memory, and consciousness.

expert.summary: Motor hierarchy within the frontal lobe: primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus), premotor area for movement planning, frontal eye fields, and Broca's area.

points.text: The premotor area plans movements; the frontal eye fields control eye movements and attention to visual stimuli.
Broca's area supports language production and the movements of speech, and in most people is present only on the left.

checks.q: Which groove separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe?
checks.explain: The lateral sulcus separates the temporal lobe; the longitudinal fissure separates the hemispheres.

beginner.summary: The parietal lobe lies behind the central sulcus. Its main job is body sensation: touch, pressure, pain, and sensing where your body is.

points.text: Its main sensation is somatosensation, the general senses of the body.
The parieto-occipital sulcus, visible on the inner (medial) surface, separates it from the occipital lobe.

expert.summary: The postcentral gyrus (Brodmann areas 1, 2 and 3) is the primary somatosensory cortex; parietal regions also join the temporal lobe in higher visual processing.

points.text: More complex visual processing extends beyond the occipital lobe into the temporal and parietal lobes.

beginner.summary: The temporal lobe sits low on the side of each hemisphere, under the lateral sulcus. It handles hearing and plays a big part in memory.

points.text: The lateral sulcus separates the temporal lobe from the lobes above it.
Primary auditory cortex (Brodmann areas 41 and 42) lies in the superior temporal lobe.
Because parts of the temporal lobe belong to the limbic system, memory is a key temporal-lobe function.

expert.summary: The medial temporal lobe houses the hippocampal formation and amygdala; select those structures for detail.

checks.q: Primary auditory cortex is found in which lobe?
checks.explain: Brodmann areas 41 and 42 lie in the superior temporal lobe.

beginner.summary: The occipital lobe is at the very back of the brain and is where vision first reaches the cortex.

points.text: Brodmann areas 17 and 18 in the occipital lobe handle primary visual perception.
On the outer surface there is no obvious border between the occipital lobe and the parietal or temporal lobes.

expert.summary: Visual processing continues beyond primary visual cortex into temporal and parietal regions.

points.text: Complex visual processing involves the temporal and parietal lobes as well as the occipital lobe.

checks.q: Primary visual perception depends on Brodmann areas 17 and 18 in which lobe?
checks.explain: Areas 17 and 18 are in the occipital lobe.

beginner.summary: This ridge, just in front of the central sulcus, sends the commands that move your muscles.

points.text: The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex.
Control is crossed: the right motor cortex controls the left side of the body.

expert.summary: Upper motor neurons here instruct spinal cord neurons that drive skeletal muscle.

points.text: Cells of this region are upper motor neurons that instruct spinal cord cells to move skeletal muscles.
Movement planning upstream involves the premotor area and the basal nuclei.

connections.label: Just anterior to the central sulcus
Partner across the sulcus: postcentral gyrus

checks.q: The right precentral gyrus mainly controls movement of which side of the body?
checks.explain: Motor control is contralateral (crossed).

beginner.summary: This ridge, just behind the central sulcus, is where body sensations first reach the cortex.

points.text: The postcentral gyrus is the primary somatosensory cortex.
It processes touch, pressure, pain, itch, vibration, and the sense of body position.

expert.summary: Corresponds to Brodmann areas 1, 2 and 3.

points.text: The primary somatosensory cortex is identified as Brodmann areas 1, 2 and 3.

connections.label: Just posterior to the central sulcus
Partner across the sulcus: precentral gyrus

checks.q: Primary somatosensory cortex corresponds to which Brodmann areas?
checks.explain: 17/18 are visual and 41/42 are auditory.

beginner.summary: A thick band of white matter deep in the brain that links the left and right hemispheres.

points.text: The corpus callosum is the major pathway for communication between the two cerebral hemispheres.

expert.summary: The largest commissural white-matter structure of the cerebrum.

beginner.summary: A set of deep nuclei that help decide whether a movement happens. Their most important job is planning movement.

points.text: The basal nuclei compare cortical activity with the overall state of the nervous system to influence whether a movement takes place.
The caudate and putamen together form the striatum, the entry point for cortical input.

expert.summary: Two opposing loops through the thalamus gate cortical excitation, and dopamine from the substantia nigra tilts the balance between them.

points.text: Direct pathway: striatum to internal globus pallidus/substantia nigra pars reticulata to thalamus to cortex. It disinhibits the thalamus, allowing cortical excitation; dopamine activates it.
Indirect pathway: striatum to external globus pallidus to subthalamic nucleus to internal globus pallidus/pars reticulata. It reinforces thalamic inhibition; dopamine inhibits it.
Substantia nigra pars compacta releases dopamine into the striatum.

checks.q: Which two nuclei together form the striatum?
checks.explain: All cortical input to the basal nuclei enters through the striatum.

checks.q: What does dopamine do to the indirect pathway?
checks.explain: Dopamine activates the direct pathway and inhibits the indirect pathway, both favoring movement.

topics.title: Thalamus

beginner.summary: The brain's central relay hub: almost every sense passes through it on the way to the cortex.

points.text: All sensory information except smell passes through the thalamus before reaching the cortex.
It does more than relay; it also processes information, for example influencing which visual stimuli get attention.

expert.summary: About 60 nuclei, grouped on each side into anterior, medial and lateral groups, plus a reticular nucleus that regulates thalamic activity.

points.text: Motor, limbic and sensory pathways (except olfaction) pass through the thalamus; it divides into roughly 60 nuclei.
On each side the nuclei form lateral, medial and anterior groups; relay nuclei make up most of the thalamus.
The reticular nucleus projects back onto the thalamus rather than to cortex, and contributes to alertness and attention.
It receives the primary output of the basal nuclei.
The intralaminar and reticular nuclei are linked to arousal and pain regulation.

connections.label: Receives hippocampal output via the fornix (anterior nuclei)

clinical.text: An anatomic variant, the artery of Percheron (estimated in 4% to 12% of people), can cause infarction of both thalami when blocked.
After a thalamic stroke, numbness and tingling on the opposite side of the body can later turn into severe chronic pain (thalamic pain syndrome, Dejerine-Roussy).
Fatal familial insomnia is a hereditary prion disease in which abnormal protein deposits in the thalamus.

checks.q: Which sense does NOT pass through the thalamus on its way to the cortex?
checks.explain: Olfaction is the exception.

topics.short: Relay hub for senses and movement

beginner.summary: A small region below the thalamus that keeps the body's internal conditions stable.

points.text: It lies below and slightly in front of the thalamus.
It largely regulates homeostasis.

expert.summary: Controls the autonomic nervous system and, through the pituitary, the endocrine system; parts contribute to limbic functions.

points.text: It controls the autonomic nervous system and the endocrine system via the anterior pituitary.
Parts of the hypothalamus contribute to memory and emotion as part of the limbic system.
The lateral hypothalamus senses hunger and increases eating.
Nuclei of the periventricular zone mainly regulate the endocrine system; those of the medial and lateral zones regulate autonomic and somatic behavior.

checks.q: The hypothalamus mainly regulates…
checks.explain: It keeps internal conditions stable through autonomic and endocrine control.

beginner.summary: A curved structure deep in the temporal lobe that is essential for turning experiences into lasting memories.

points.text: The hippocampus is closely associated with consolidating memories and with decision-making.
It and the amygdala are involved in forming long-term memories and emotional responses.

expert.summary: Three zones (dentate gyrus, hippocampus proper, subiculum); Cornu Ammonis subfields CA1 to CA4; main output via the fornix.

points.text: It lies within the parahippocampal gyrus and bulges into the temporal (inferior) horn of the lateral ventricle.
Its three zones are the dentate gyrus, the hippocampus proper, and the subiculum.
The Cornu Ammonis is divided into subfields CA1, CA2, CA3 and CA4; CA3 receives input from dentate granule cells.
The fornix is its main outflow bundle, projecting toward the anterior thalamus and hypothalamus.

connections.label: Bulges into: temporal horn of lateral ventricle

clinical.text: Alzheimer's disease involves early loss of synapses in the hippocampus, and loss of CA1 pyramidal neurons; these changes may contribute to memory loss.
In medial temporal lobe epilepsy caused by hippocampal sclerosis, surgeons may remove the hippocampus (hippocampectomy).
After both hippocampi were largely removed to treat epilepsy, the patient H.M. could no longer form new memories (anterograde amnesia).

checks.q: The hippocampus is best known for its role in…
checks.explain: It is central to memory consolidation.

checks.q: What is the main output bundle of the hippocampus?
checks.explain: The fornix carries hippocampal output toward the anterior thalamus and hypothalamus.

beginner.summary: An almond-shaped cluster deep in the temporal lobe that helps process emotions, especially fear.

points.text: The amygdala is almond-shaped and lies in the temporal lobe, just beneath the uncus.
It helps regulate anxiety, aggression, fear conditioning, emotional memory, and social cognition.

expert.summary: About 13 nuclei in five functional groups; outputs reach the septal area, hypothalamus and mediodorsal thalamus.

points.text: Its roughly 13 nuclei sort into basolateral, cortical-like, central, other amygdaloid, and extended amygdala groups.
A dorsal output route (stria terminalis) reaches the septal area and hypothalamus; a ventral route (ventral amygdalofugal pathway) also reaches the mediodorsal thalamic nucleus.
Amygdala activation modulates how emotionally charged memories are acquired and consolidated.

clinical.text: Bilateral reductions of hippocampal and amygdala volume have been reported in PTSD.
Klüver-Bucy syndrome, a rare behavioral syndrome, can follow damage to both amygdalae.

checks.q: The amygdala is most associated with…
checks.explain: It processes fear, anxiety and emotional memory.

topics.title: Midbrain

beginner.summary: The top part of the brain stem, between the thalamus and the pons.

points.text: The brain stem (midbrain, pons, medulla) connects the forebrain to the spinal cord.
The midbrain coordinates maps of visual, auditory and body-sense space.

expert.summary: Roof (tectum) with the colliculi; floor (tegmentum); the cerebral aqueduct runs through its center.

points.text: The superior colliculus integrates visual, auditory and somatosensory input and orients the eyes toward a sound or touch.
The inferior colliculus is part of the auditory brain stem pathway and projects to the thalamus.
The cerebral aqueduct passes through the midbrain.

topics.short: Top of the brain stem; eye and ear reflexes

beginner.summary: The bulge in the middle of the brain stem; its name means bridge.

points.text: Seen from the front it is a thick bundle of white matter, the main connection to the cerebellum.

expert.summary: Pontine neurons relay descending forebrain input to the cerebellum.

points.text: Neurons in the pons relay descending forebrain input, including copies of motor commands, to the cerebellum.

beginner.summary: The lowest part of the brain stem, continuous with the spinal cord. It helps keep you breathing and your heart working.

points.text: Its white matter is continuous with the spinal cord.
It regulates cardiovascular and respiratory functions.

expert.summary: Contains cranial nerve nuclei and the inferior olive, which sends sensory input to the cerebellum.

points.text: It contains nuclei that process cranial nerve information, including the inferior olive.

checks.q: Which part of the brain stem regulates breathing and heart function?
checks.explain: The medulla regulates cardiovascular and respiratory functions.

beginner.summary: The 'little brain' at the back and bottom. It compares what you meant to do with what your body actually did, and corrects movement.

points.text: It is about 10 percent of the brain's mass and is folded like the cerebrum.
It compares motor commands from the cerebrum with sensory feedback to correct and coordinate movement.
Damage impairs fine movement control, posture, and motor learning.

expert.summary: Two hemispheres joined by the vermis; three lobes; three-layer cortex; deep nuclei provide the output.

points.text: Two hemispheres are joined by the vermis; the primary and posterolateral fissures divide it into anterior, posterior and flocculonodular lobes.
The cortex has three layers: molecular, Purkinje cell, and granular.
Deep nuclei, medial to lateral: fastigial, interposed (globose and emboliform), and dentate, the largest.
Superior, middle and inferior cerebellar peduncles attach it to the brain stem.
It receives motor-command copies via pontine neurons and sensory input via the inferior olive, and sends corrections to the midbrain.

Three functional zones: vestibulocerebellum (balance and eye control), spinocerebellum (vermis and paravermis: muscle tone and coordination) and cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres: planning and timing).

clinical.text: Cerebellar damage typically causes clumsy, poorly coordinated movement (ataxia) on the same side as the damage.

checks.q: The cerebellum's main job is to…
checks.explain: It compares intended movement with feedback and corrects it.

checks.q: Which is the largest deep cerebellar nucleus?
checks.explain: From medial to lateral: fastigial, interposed, dentate (largest).

beginner.summary: Fluid-filled spaces inside the brain, left over from the hollow tube the nervous system develops from.

points.text: Lateral ventricles sit in the hemispheres, the third ventricle in the diencephalon, and the fourth in the hindbrain.
The diencephalon forms the walls of the third ventricle.

expert.summary: The fourth ventricle continues into the spinal cord's central canal; the cerebral aqueduct links third and fourth ventricles through the midbrain.

points.text: The spinal cord's central canal is continuous with the fourth ventricle and filled with cerebrospinal fluid.

topics.title: Anterior thalamic nucleus
topics.short: Memory relay of the limbic system

beginner.summary: A nucleus at the front of the thalamus that helps you remember events.

points.text: Its connections with the hippocampus, mammillary bodies and fornix let the thalamus contribute to learning and memory of events (episodic memory).

expert.summary: A nucleus at the front of the thalamus that helps you remember events.

points.text: It belongs to the anterior nuclear group, one of the relay groups separated by the internal medullary lamina.
The mammillary bodies, a hub of limbic memory circuits, connect with the anterior thalamic nuclei.

checks.q: The anterior thalamic nucleus mainly supports…
checks.explain: Its limbic connections support episodic memory.

beginner.summary: A large nucleus in the middle part of the thalamus linked to emotion.

points.text: It is thought to help process emotion and coordinate attention to painful (noxious) information.

expert.summary: A large nucleus in the middle part of the thalamus linked to emotion.

beginner.summary: Part of the intralaminar nuclei, buried inside the internal medullary lamina.

points.text: Intralaminar nuclei are linked to arousal and to regulating pain.

expert.summary: Part of the intralaminar nuclei, buried inside the internal medullary lamina.

points.text: Intralaminar nuclei receive input from the basal ganglia and project to the cortex.

beginner.summary: One of the thalamus's two main motor nuclei, together with the ventral lateral nucleus.

points.text: The ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei are the thalamus's motor nuclei.

expert.summary: One of the thalamus's two main motor nuclei, together with the ventral lateral nucleus.

points.text: It is a relay nucleus of the lateral (ventral) nuclear group.

topics.title: Ventral lateral nucleus (VL)
topics.short: Relays cerebellum and basal ganglia to motor cortex

beginner.summary: A motor relay: it passes signals from movement-control centers to the motor cortex.

points.text: It receives input from the cerebellum and basal ganglia and relays motor information to the precentral (motor) cortex.

expert.summary: A motor relay: it passes signals from movement-control centers to the motor cortex.

points.text: The cerebrocerebellum's output reaches the thalamus through the dentate and interposed nuclei.

checks.q: The ventral lateral nucleus relays input from the cerebellum and basal ganglia to…
checks.explain: VL relays motor information to the precentral gyrus.

beginner.summary: Relays touch, pain and temperature from the body to the sensory cortex.

points.text: It receives spinal sensory pathways carrying temperature, pain, vibration, pressure, fine touch and body position, and relays them to the primary somatosensory cortex.

expert.summary: Relays touch, pain and temperature from the body to the sensory cortex.

checks.q: VPL relays sensation from the body to…
checks.explain: VPL projects to the postcentral gyrus.

beginner.summary: Relays sensation from the face, and taste, to the sensory cortex.

points.text: It receives the trigeminal (face) and taste pathways and relays facial sensation and taste to the primary somatosensory cortex.

expert.summary: Relays sensation from the face, and taste, to the sensory cortex.

checks.q: Which thalamic nucleus relays facial sensation and taste?
checks.explain: VPM handles the trigeminal and taste pathways; VPL handles the body.

beginner.summary: A relay nucleus near the top of the thalamus.

points.text: It is a relay nucleus of the lateral nuclear group.
Together with the anterior nucleus it makes up the upper, front region of the thalamus.

expert.summary: A relay nucleus near the top of the thalamus.

beginner.summary: A relay nucleus in the back part of the thalamus, next to the pulvinar.

points.text: It is a relay nucleus of the lateral nuclear group.

expert.summary: A relay nucleus in the back part of the thalamus, next to the pulvinar.

beginner.summary: A large nucleus at the back of the thalamus.

points.text: It makes up about 30 percent of the thalamus's volume in humans.
Its main roles involve combining information from several senses and orienting behavior.

expert.summary: A large nucleus at the back of the thalamus.

beginner.summary: The thalamus's vision relay.

points.text: It receives visual signals from the optic tract and relays them to the primary visual cortex along the calcarine sulcus.

expert.summary: The thalamus's vision relay.

checks.q: The lateral geniculate nucleus relays…
checks.explain: LGN relays optic tract input to the visual cortex.

beginner.summary: The thalamus's hearing relay.

points.text: It receives auditory input from the superior olive and inferior colliculus and relays it to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.

expert.summary: The thalamus's hearing relay.

checks.q: The medial geniculate nucleus relays…
checks.explain: MGN relays auditory signals to the temporal lobe.

beginner.summary: Not a nucleus: a Y-shaped sheet of fibers inside the thalamus.

points.text: On each side it separates the lateral, medial and anterior nuclear groups.

expert.summary: Not a nucleus: a Y-shaped sheet of fibers inside the thalamus.

beginner.summary: A short fiber bundle connecting the mammillary bodies to the thalamus.

points.text: Through this tract the thalamus connects with limbic memory structures.

expert.summary: A short fiber bundle connecting the mammillary bodies to the thalamus.

clinical.text: In Korsakoff syndrome, damage to the mammillary bodies can extend into the thalamus through the mammillothalamic fasciculus.

topics.title: Caudate nucleus
topics.short: Part of the striatum (movement and learning input)

beginner.summary: A long, C-shaped nucleus that curves alongside the lateral ventricle.

points.text: It runs from the frontal lobe back and down into the temporal lobe.
With the putamen it forms the striatum, where cortical input enters the basal nuclei.

expert.summary: A long, C-shaped nucleus that curves alongside the lateral ventricle.

beginner.summary: A rounded nucleus deep in the hemisphere, lateral to the globus pallidus.

points.text: It lies mostly deep to the anterior frontal and parietal regions.
With the caudate it forms the striatum, the input stage of the basal nuclei.

expert.summary: A rounded nucleus deep in the hemisphere, lateral to the globus pallidus.

beginner.summary: The outer part of the globus pallidus.

points.text: In the indirect pathway, the striatum signals the external globus pallidus, which signals the subthalamic nucleus.

expert.summary: The outer part of the globus pallidus.

topics.title: Globus pallidus, internal segment (GPi)
topics.short: Main output of the basal nuclei

beginner.summary: The inner part of the globus pallidus, an output station of the basal nuclei.

points.text: Together with the substantia nigra pars reticulata it is an output nucleus projecting to the thalamus.

expert.summary: The inner part of the globus pallidus, an output station of the basal nuclei.

beginner.summary: A small lens-shaped nucleus below the thalamus.

points.text: In the indirect pathway it relays signals from the external to the internal globus pallidus.
It lies in the subthalamus, part of the diencephalon.

expert.summary: A small lens-shaped nucleus below the thalamus.

beginner.summary: A dark band in the midbrain that supplies dopamine to the striatum.

points.text: Its pars compacta releases dopamine into the striatum; its pars reticulata is an output nucleus.

expert.summary: A dark band in the midbrain that supplies dopamine to the striatum.

points.text: Dopamine activates the direct pathway and inhibits the indirect pathway.

beginner.summary: A small nucleus where emotion and motivation meet action.

points.text: It connects with the hypothalamus, ventral tegmental area, hippocampus and amygdala in a network that supports behaviors like food-seeking and escaping predators, described as the limbic-motor interface.

expert.summary: A small nucleus where emotion and motivation meet action.

beginner.summary: A curved band of cortex just above the corpus callosum.

points.text: It sits directly above the corpus callosum.
It contributes to emotion, learning and memory, and links behavior to motivational outcomes.

expert.summary: A curved band of cortex just above the corpus callosum.

beginner.summary: The cortex wrapped around the hippocampus on the inner temporal lobe.

points.text: It supports scene recognition and the encoding and retrieval of memories.

expert.summary: The cortex wrapped around the hippocampus on the inner temporal lobe.

topics.title: Fornix
topics.short: Main output tract of the hippocampus

beginner.summary: An arching bundle of fibers carrying signals out of the hippocampus.

points.text: It is the main output tract of the hippocampus.
Its columns end in the mammillary bodies.

expert.summary: An arching bundle of fibers carrying signals out of the hippocampus.

clinical.text: Lesions along the fornix impair recall memory.

beginner.summary: Two small round bumps on the underside of the brain, part of memory circuits.

points.text: They are important for episodic memory and connect with the amygdala, hippocampus and anterior thalamic nuclei.

expert.summary: Two small round bumps on the underside of the brain, part of memory circuits.

clinical.text: Thiamine deficiency can damage them, most notably in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

checks.q: The mammillary bodies are most important for…
checks.explain: They are a hub of limbic memory circuits.

topics.title: Vermis (spinocerebellum)
topics.short: Trunk posture, gait and eye movements

beginner.summary: The narrow midline strip joining the two cerebellar hemispheres.

points.text: As part of the spinocerebellum, it receives body sensation and coordinates movement and muscle tone of the trunk, head and proximal limbs.

expert.summary: The narrow midline strip joining the two cerebellar hemispheres.

clinical.text: Vermis lesions cause truncal or gait ataxia: unsteady posture and walking.

beginner.summary: The inner strip of each cerebellar hemisphere, next to the vermis.

points.text: Also part of the spinocerebellum, the paravermis coordinates the distal limbs.

expert.summary: The inner strip of each cerebellar hemisphere, next to the vermis.

beginner.summary: The large outer parts of the cerebellar hemispheres.

points.text: They receive input from motor and supplementary motor cortex via the pons and contribute to planning, timing and coordinating movement.

expert.summary: The large outer parts of the cerebellar hemispheres.

clinical.text: Hemisphere lesions cause limb ataxia, with dysmetria (over- or undershooting a target) and intention tremor, on the same side as the lesion.

checks.q: A lesion of the left cerebellar hemisphere usually causes limb ataxia on which side?
checks.explain: Cerebellar lesions typically cause ipsilateral deficits.

topics.title: Dentate nucleus
topics.short: Output nucleus of the lateral cerebellum

beginner.summary: One of the four pairs of deep cerebellar nuclei, inside each hemisphere.

points.text: The cerebellum has four pairs of deep nuclei, which carry most of its output.

expert.summary: One of the four pairs of deep cerebellar nuclei, inside each hemisphere.

points.text: Cerebrocerebellar output leaves through the dentate and interposed nuclei toward the red nucleus and thalamus.

beginner.summary: The other deep cerebellar nuclei, medial to the dentate.

points.text: The emboliform and globose nuclei together are called the interposed nuclei; with the fastigial and dentate nuclei they are the main output route of the cerebellum.

expert.summary: The other deep cerebellar nuclei, medial to the dentate.

points.text: The fastigial nuclei are linked to saccadic and vergence eye movements.

beginner.summary: The front region of the hypothalamus, above the optic chiasm.

points.text: It contains the preoptic, paraventricular, supraoptic, suprachiasmatic and anterior hypothalamic nuclei.
The suprachiasmatic nucleus receives input from the retina and synchronizes body functions with light and dark (the circadian rhythm).
The supraoptic nucleus mainly produces vasopressin; the anterior hypothalamic nucleus helps cool the body.

expert.summary: The front region of the hypothalamus, above the optic chiasm.

checks.q: Which hypothalamic nucleus sets the body's daily rhythm from light input?
checks.explain: It receives direct retinal input.

beginner.summary: The middle region of the hypothalamus, above the pituitary stalk.

points.text: It contains the arcuate, ventromedial and dorsomedial nuclei.
The dorsomedial nucleus is involved with blood pressure, heart rate and gastrointestinal stimulation.

expert.summary: The middle region of the hypothalamus, above the pituitary stalk.

topics.title: Posterior hypothalamus
topics.short: Heat conservation and arousal of the body

beginner.summary: The back region of the hypothalamus, above the mammillary bodies.

points.text: The posterior hypothalamic nucleus helps regulate blood pressure, pupil dilation and heat conservation, such as shivering in the cold.

expert.summary: The back region of the hypothalamus, above the mammillary bodies.

points.text: The posterior region also contains the mammillary nucleus, part of the limbic system.

beginner.summary: The top-most horizontal ridge of the frontal lobe.

points.text: On the dominant (usually left) side it is a key part of the network for working memory and spatial processing.
On the non-dominant side it is involved in impulse control.

expert.summary: The top-most horizontal ridge of the frontal lobe.

beginner.summary: The middle horizontal ridge of the frontal lobe.

points.text: The dominant (left) middle frontal gyrus plays a key role in literacy; the non-dominant (right) one in numeracy.
Its back part contains the frontal eye fields (Brodmann area 8), which control fast scanning eye movements (saccades).

expert.summary: The middle horizontal ridge of the frontal lobe.

beginner.summary: The lowest ridge of the frontal lobe; on the left it contains Broca's area.

points.text: The back part of the dominant (usually left) inferior frontal gyrus contains Broca's area (Brodmann areas 44 and 45), responsible for speech production.

expert.summary: The lowest ridge of the frontal lobe; on the left it contains Broca's area.

checks.q: Broca's area, important for producing speech, is in which gyrus?
checks.explain: It lies in the caudal part of the dominant inferior frontal gyrus.

beginner.summary: The very front tip of the frontal lobe, part of the prefrontal cortex.

points.text: The prefrontal cortex is a higher-order association center for decision making and personality.

expert.summary: The very front tip of the frontal lobe, part of the prefrontal cortex.

beginner.summary: The upper part of the parietal lobe behind the postcentral gyrus.

points.text: It contains somatosensory association cortex (Brodmann areas 5 and 7) involved in higher functions such as planning actions.

expert.summary: The upper part of the parietal lobe behind the postcentral gyrus.

beginner.summary: The lower part of the parietal lobe, including the supramarginal and angular gyri.

points.text: It includes the supramarginal gyrus (Brodmann area 40) and angular gyrus (area 39), and contains the secondary somatosensory cortex, which integrates input from the thalamus.

expert.summary: The lower part of the parietal lobe, including the supramarginal and angular gyri.

beginner.summary: The top ridge of the temporal lobe, just below the lateral sulcus.

points.text: It supports phonological representation, the sound structure of heard words; Wernicke's area lies in the dominant superior temporal gyrus.

expert.summary: The top ridge of the temporal lobe, just below the lateral sulcus.

beginner.summary: The middle ridge of the temporal lobe.

points.text: Part of it belongs to a semantic control network that assigns meaning to words and sounds.

expert.summary: The middle ridge of the temporal lobe.

beginner.summary: The lowest ridge on the side of the temporal lobe.

points.text: It contributes to visual and face perception as part of the ventral visual pathway, which carries information from primary visual cortex to identify what is seen.

expert.summary: The lowest ridge on the side of the temporal lobe.

beginner.summary: A bump on the back of the midbrain.

points.text: It integrates visual, auditory and body-sense information and orients the eyes toward a sound or touch.

expert.summary: A bump on the back of the midbrain.

beginner.summary: A bump on the back of the midbrain, below the superior colliculus.

points.text: It is part of the auditory pathway and projects to the thalamus, which relays sound to the cerebrum.

expert.summary: A bump on the back of the midbrain, below the superior colliculus.

steps.predict: Before we start: how many major regions do you think the brain is divided into?
steps.text: Anatomists describe four major regions: cerebrum, diencephalon, brain stem, and cerebellum. This tour visits each one.
From above you see the cerebrum's two hemispheres, separated by the longitudinal fissure. The wrinkled surface is the cerebral cortex.

steps.predict: The two hemispheres need to talk. Where do you think the bridge between them is?
steps.text: Deep in the middle, the corpus callosum carries most of the traffic between the hemispheres.
The frontal lobe: movement, planning, and much of what we call personality.
The central sulcus divides frontal from parietal. In front of it, the precentral gyrus moves the body; behind it, the postcentral gyrus feels the body.
The temporal lobe, below the lateral sulcus: hearing and memory.
The occipital lobe at the back is where vision first reaches the cortex.
The diencephalon sits at the center. The thalamus relays almost all senses to the cortex; the hypothalamus keeps the body in balance.

steps.predict: Which region do you think keeps you breathing without thinking about it?
steps.text: The brain stem: midbrain, pons, and medulla. The medulla regulates breathing and heart function.
The cerebellum compares intended movement with what actually happened and corrects it. You now know the four regions; try the Quiz to lock them in.
Commands start in the primary motor cortex, whose upper motor neurons instruct the spinal cord.

steps.predict: Which deep structures do you think decide whether a movement is allowed to start?
steps.text: The basal nuclei gate movement. Cortical input enters the striatum (caudate and putamen).
Dopamine from the substantia nigra activates the direct pathway and inhibits the indirect pathway.
Basal nuclei output returns to the cortex through the thalamus.
Copies of motor commands travel through the pons to the cerebellum.
The cerebellum compares the command with sensory feedback (via the inferior olive) and sends corrections to the midbrain.

steps.predict: Where do you think new long-term memories are formed? Look at the inside of the temporal lobe.
steps.text: The hippocampus, deep in the temporal lobe, is central to forming lasting memories.
Its main output is the fornix, an arching bundle heading toward the anterior thalamus and hypothalamus.
Just in front of the hippocampus, the amygdala processes fear and adds emotional weight to memories.
The amygdala reaches the hypothalamus, which drives the body's autonomic and hormonal responses.

tours.title: From eye to sight: the visual pathway

steps.predict: Where in the brain do you think seeing happens: just behind the eyes, or somewhere else?
steps.text: Light is detected in the retina at the back of each eye, but seeing happens much farther back, in the visual cortex of the occipital lobe. This tour follows the signal there.
Each retina sends its signals out of the eye along an optic nerve.

steps.predict: Does each eye report only to its own side of the brain?
steps.text: The two optic nerves meet at the optic chiasm. Fibres from the nose-side half of each retina cross to the other side here; fibres from the outer half stay on their own side.

Behind the chiasm the fibres continue as the optic tracts. Because of the partial crossing, each side of the brain now carries the opposite half of what you see: the left side handles the right half of your view.
Most optic tract fibres end in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, the relay station on the way to the cortex.
Some fibres go to the superior colliculus in the midbrain instead. It combines sight, sound and touch and helps turn the head toward something that grabs your attention.

steps.predict: If something is at the top of your view, do you think the top or the bottom of the visual cortex handles it?
steps.text: Neurons in the lateral geniculate nucleus send their axons to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe, mostly on its inner wall along the calcarine sulcus. The map is flipped: the upper part of the visual cortex handles the lower part of your view.

From the visual cortex, information flows along two streams. A lower stream into the temporal lobe works out what you are looking at; an upper stream into the parietal lobe works out where it is and guides your movements.

tours.title: How a sound reaches the cortex

steps.predict: A sound arrives at your right ear a split second before your left. What could the brain use that for?
steps.text: Signals from the inner ear enter the brain stem at the cochlear nuclei, in the upper medulla. Brain stem nuclei then combine input from both ears and use the small differences in timing and loudness to work out where a sound came from.
Auditory signals continue up to the inferior colliculus in the midbrain.
One branch goes to the superior colliculus, which helps turn your head and neck toward the sound.
The main branch goes to the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, the relay for hearing.
The medial geniculate nucleus passes the signal to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe, where sound is consciously heard.

steps.predict: If you touch something with your left hand, which side of the brain do you think feels it?
steps.text: Fine touch and body-position signals climb the back of the spinal cord in the dorsal column system and reach two nuclei in the medulla, the nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus. The next neuron's axon crosses the midline here, so touch on the left side of the body is handled by the right side of the brain.
After crossing, the axons rise through the brain stem as a bundle called the medial lemniscus and end in the thalamus, where they connect with the third neuron of the pathway.
The third neuron projects to the postcentral gyrus, where the touch is first processed by the cortex and becomes a conscious sensation.

steps.predict: Do you think your back or your fingertips get more cortex?
steps.text: The postcentral gyrus holds a map of the body, but not a scale model: sensitive areas such as the fingers and lower face take up far more cortex than the shoulders and back.
Pain and temperature take a different route, the spinothalamic tract, which crosses in the spinal cord at the level where the signal enters instead of in the medulla.
